Keywords: Imbalanced learning Multiclass classification One-versus-one decomposition Spectral clustering

## a b s t r a c t

In many real-world applications, an algorithm needs to learn multiclass classification models from data with imbalanced class distributions. Multiclass imbalanced learning is currently receiving increased attention from researchers. In contrast to traditional imbalanced learning on binary datasets, multiclass imbalanced learning faces great challenges from the variety of changes in the class distributions as well as the inadequate performance of multiclass classification algorithms. In this paper, we propose a novel data preprocessing-based method to solve this problem. The proposed method combines a one-versusone (OVO) decomposition of class pairs and a spectral clustering technique. This method first decomposes a multiclass dataset into several binary-class datasets. Then, it uses spectral clustering to divide the minority classes of binary-class subsets into subspaces and oversamples them according to the characteristics of the data. Sampling based on spectral clustering takes into account the distribution of the data and effectively avoids oversampling outliers. After the data approximately reaches the equilibrium point, multiclass classifiers can be trained from these rebalanced data. We compared the proposed method with five state-of-the-art multiclass imbalanced learning methods on seven multiclass datasets, using multi-class area under the ROC curve (MAUC), the precision of minor classes $( P _ { m i n } )$ and the average precision of all classes $( P _ { a v g } )$ as the performance metrics. The experimental results show that our proposed method has the best overall performance.

## 1. Introduction

Classification is one of the core tasks in the field of machine learning. Traditional classification algorithms have been developed for many years and they have achieved high performance levels in several application domains. In the era of big data, tremendous amounts of data have rapidly accumulated in various application systems, which makes the problem of imbalanced learning increasingly prominent. It is widely known that the performance of traditional classification algorithms probably deteriorates when running on imbalanced datasets (He & Garcia, 2008). The big gaps in the number of samples for different classes usually skews the pre-diction of classifiers toward the majority groups. That is, unlabeled examples, belonging to minor classes, are often misclassified into majority classes (Jiang, Li, Cai & Zhang, 2013). However, from the application perspective, minority groups are usually more important than the majority groups because they represent a class of information that is rare but must be taken seriously (B. B. Krawczyk, 2016; Liang, Zhang, Sivasubramaniam, Jette & Sahoo, 2006). For example, in the case of credit card fraud detection, among the massive amounts of credit card usage information, only a very small portion is abnormal (Zhou, Hu, Li & Wu, 2017). In the case of medical diagnoses, only a small quantity of the vast amounts of medical diagnostic images has been diagnosed as showing cancer. In both of these cases, the minor-class cases are significant but the misclassification of them is costly. A similar situation exists for multi-class imbalanced data. For example, in the protein fold problem (Zhao, Li, Chen & Aihara, 2008), the SCOP dataset contains 701 folds, while the number of proteins in each fold varies greatly. In the weld flaws problem (Liao, 2008), there are relatively few instances of defective welds. In addition, different types of weld defects may be unevenly distributed.

In the past two decades, many studies have been conducted to address class imbalanced learning problems and great progress has been made in the case of binary classification. However, as we know, multiclass imbalanced learning is more common in practice and is intuitively more difficult to handle. On the one hand, the gaps of sample sizes among the multiple classes are large so the imbalanced conditions are more complicated than in the binary cases. On the other hand, the peripheral contour of the samples is more blurred. For example, in a binary-class imbalanced dataset, the minor-class examples at the boundary are only surrounded by one other class, while the examples may be surrounded by several other classes simultaneously in a multiclass imbalanced problem. Therefore, either it is invalid to directly apply the methods for binary-class imbalanced problems to multiclass imbalanced issues, or the performance of these algorithms will be lower under multi-ple skewed datasets.

To handle the multiclass issue, a common strategy is to divide the original problem into a set of atomic sub-problems that are solvable by existing binary-class learning techniques (Fernández, Del Jesus & Herrera, 2010). The most popular decomposition methods are one-versus-one (OVO) and one-versusall (OVA). Although the decomposition process of OVA is simpler than OVO, there is a big drawback to running this decomposition on imbalanced datasets. That is, when the examples belonging to the classes that are not “small” enough are combined as one class, it results in an extremely uneven distribution if the remaining class is a minor class. Therefore, OVA is not reliable for handling problems with distributions that are initially skewed (Zhang, Krawczyk, Garcìa, Rosales-Pérez & Herrera, 2016). Fernández, López, Galar, Del Jesus and Herrera (2013) empirically studied OVO and OVA decompositions using several standard machine-learning algorithms to address the multiclass learning problems. Their experimental results showed that OVO significantly outperforms OVA. In this study, we also take advantage of the OVO decomposition strategy to deal with multiclass imbalanced learning problems.

To handle an imbalanced class distribution, we usually resample the original data to reach a balance so that classifiers can be induced from the new balanced dataset. At present, most resampling algorithms are based on the distance between two data points. They simply perform the same sampling strategy on all data points without considering the different distributions of the data points in the same class. For example, the SMOTE algorithm (Chawla, Bowyer, Hall & Kegelmeyer, 2002) calculates the sample point and its k-nearest neighbors based on the Euclidean distance, and then randomly synthesizes a new sample on the two-point line. These simple sampling strategies usually cause the samples on the class boundaries to be sampled multiple times, which easily results in the overlapping of the minor class and major class, so that the boundaries of the classes are more ambiguous than before the sampling. For the multiclass imbalanced datasets, the simple sampling strategies are even less competent because of a more complicated data distribution. A more sophisticated sampling strategy is required, which takes into account the inner-class data distribution. Furthermore, sampling techniques can be divided into two categories undersampling and oversampling according to the method decreasing or increasing the number of sampled classes. Since undersampling tends to discard some important information in the classifier induction process (B. B. Krawczyk, 2016), our study adopts the oversampling technique.

In this paper, we propose a novel data-level method for multiclass imbalanced classification by combining the OVO decomposition method and an oversampling technique with spectral clustering. We use spectral clustering to guide the oversampling process. Compared with the commonly used k-means clustering that assumes the data points in a cluster form a convex set (Von Luxburg, 2007), spectral clustering relaxes this strong assumption. It can efficiently partition the data space and group similar data points into the same cluster even if the data distributions are complex. In our proposed method, the synthesized samples will be limited to a dense space in the minority class regions, which alleviates the overlapping between different classes, which makes the subsequent classification models more effective.

To evaluate the performance of our proposed method, we conducted comprehensive experiments on eleven multiclass imbalanced datasets taken from the UCI,<sup>1</sup> KEEL<sup>2</sup> and OpenML<sup>3</sup> data repositories made comparisons with five state-of-the-art OVO decomposition-based methods. The experimental results show that our method achieves the best overall performance. The contributions of this paper are three-fold:

• We propose a novel multiclass imbalanced learning method that combines the OVO decomposition method and oversampling with spectral clustering.

• We conduct a comprehensive experiment to evaluate the performance of our proposed algorithm by comparisons with five state-of-the-art algorithms drawn from the research literature. These compared algorithms are all the best ones from the original research articles but have never been compared together.

• We use several evaluation metrics and carefully tune the imbalance ratios of the datasets, which verify the reliability of the proposed method.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 briefly reviews the related studies. In Section 3, we present our proposed method that combines the OVO decomposition method and oversampling with spectral clustering. Section 4 presents the experimental setup, the results and analysis. Section 5 concludes the paper and points to future research.

## 2. Background

Current solutions for imbalance learning can be classified into three categories: data-level methods, algorithm-level methods, and ensemble methods. The data-level methods recommend processing the original data to rebalance the class distribution. The algorithmlevel methods attempt to adapt existing classifiers to imbalanced datasets and bias to the minority class, which is primarily based on cost-sensitive mechanisms. However, in many cases, these costs are not available. The ensemble methods combine the efficient ensemble learning solutions with previously mentioned strategies above, especially with classifier ensembles. In this paper, we focus on the data level solutions because it is more flexible, and its usage is independent of the classifier selected. We may preprocess all datasets once to use them for training different classifiers.

In this section, we first review the resampling techniques, which is the basis of many data-level methods used in imbalanced learning. Then, we review the decomposition methods used for multiclass classification. Finally, we describe the spectral clustering algorithm used in our method.

## 2.1. Resampling methods

In general, resampling methods can be divided into three categories: oversampling, undersampling, and hybrid ones. The most intuitive method is to randomly replicate the minority class examples or randomly eliminate majority examples to rebalance the class distribution artificially; this is called random oversampling (ROS) and random undersampling (RUS). It seems that ROS and RUS solve the problem of imbalanced learning to a certain extent, but both methods also introduce new problems. The huge drawback to random undersampling is that some potentially useful information will be missed when the data are randomly removed, which ultimately misleads the classification. Therefore, finding ways to remove major-class samples without affecting the induction process has become an important issue. To handle the deficiencies caused by the loss of multiclass of information introduced by RUS, the EasyEnsemble and the BalanceCascade (Liu, Wu & Zhou, 2009) heuristic-based methods are proposed. Both of methods effectively utilize potentially useful majority sample information that is ignored by random undersampling. EasyEnsemble performs multiple independent random undersampling processes on the majority class samples to obtain multiple subsets, each of which has the same number of samples as the minority class. Each subset and minority class sample are combined into a new balanced training set and are trained to obtain the AdaBoost classifier and the weak AdaBoost classifiers are assembled. Unlike the multiple independent samplings of the EasyEnsemble algorithm, the BalanceCascade uses a supervised method for random undersampling of the major classes. After using the random undersampling algorithm to create the balanced dataset and learning the AdaBoost classifier in each round, some of the correctly classified samples in the majority class are removed as redundant information. Therefore, the remaining samples are retained as the most valuable information. Both of the algorithms make full use of the major classes’ sample information. In addition, a new adaptive undersampling method has also been proposed, which guides the sampling process based on a differential evolution algorithm to reduce the total error classification cost (Qiu, Jiang & Kong, 2015).

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">2 [https://sci2s.ugr.es/keel/datasets.php.](https://sci2s.ugr.es/keel/datasets.php)</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">3 [https://www.openml.org/search?type=data.](https://www.openml.org/search?type=data)</span></small>

Random oversampling increases the risk of overfitting. A powerful method to balance the class distribution and avoid overfitting is SMOTE. Unlike the ROS random duplicate examples, SMOTE creates a synthetic sample using the original samples. The algorithm randomly selects one of its k-nearest neighbors from the minority class and generates new minority instances by linear interpolation. However, SMOTE also has its drawbacks, such as overgeneralizations and variances, and it can increase the overlap between different classes and worsen the decision boundaries, especially in multiclass cases. Various adaptive sampling methods have been proposed to overcome this limitation. Significant work in this area includes the Borderline-SMOTE (Han, Wang & Mao, 2005), Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (ADASYN) (He, Bai, Garcia & Li, 2008) algorithms and SMOTEBoost (Chawla, Lazarevic, Hall & Bowyer, 2003). The difference between the Borderline-SMOTE, the SMOTE algorithm and the ADASYN algorithm is that the SMOTE algorithms only generate new samples for critical minority class samples and removes noise samples, while the ADASYN adaptively generates different numbers of new samples for each minor class according to the class distribution. The number of generated samples is proportional to the size of the majority class sample in the neighborhood. However, the ADASYN does not consider the noise samples, which makes it is easy to generate samples in the wrong area and make a misjudgment. SMOTEBoost integrates resampling strategy with ensemble learning technology. Specifically, SMOTEBoost introduces SMOTE for each boost process. In this way, every successive classifier set is able to focus more on the minority classes. Different from the methods mentioned above, Abdi and Hashemi (2015) proposed a resampling method for multiclass learning under class skew, namely Mahalanobis Distancebased Over-sampling (MDO), which generates synthetic samples that have the same Mahalanobis distance from the class mean as other minority class examples.

## 2.2. Decompositions for multiclass classification

One possible research direction is to solve multiclass imbalanced learning by using the rule of divide and conquer to decompose the multiclass problem into binary-class sub-problems and then apply the binary-class imbalanced learning algorithms to these sub-problems. The main types of decomposition methods are OVO and OVA. However, the imbalanced situation may worsen in OVA because it aggravates the imbalance rate between classes. Fernández et al. (2013) studied the OVO and OVA decompositions using standard machine-learning algorithms to address the multiple class learning problems, their experimental results showed that OVO outperforms OVA. Therefore, most studies emphasize the importance of the OVO strategy and the OVO strategy is recommended for applications in an imbalanced situation. Large proportions of the research tend to utilize the resampling techniques with an OVO strategy for multiclass imbalanced problems. Our previous work (Song, Zhang, Yan & Li, 2018) presents an empirical study on state-of-the-art multiclass imbalanced learning algorithms, which are based on one-versus-one (OVO) decomposition, comparing their performance on multiclass imbalanced datasets. Fernández et al. (2010) decomposed an original dataset into binary sub-datasets and then rebalanced them by oversampling. Krawczyk (2015) combined the OVO decomposition with SMOTE and Underbagging, which is a combination of resampling methods and the bagging ensemble algorithm. Vluymans, Fernández, Saeys, Cornelis and Herrera (2018) considered the IFROWANN’s extension to multiclass data by combining it with the OVO decomposition. The abovementioned methods have shown their effectiveness in multiclass imbalanced problems. Thus, the OVO strategy will be employed in this paper.

## 2.3. Spectral clustering

Spectral clustering (Von Luxburg, 2007) is a relatively modern clustering method that evolved from spectral theory and was later widely used in clustering due to its excellent performance. It is based on standard linear algebra methods and is simple to implement. Compared with other traditional clustering methods, such as the k-means method, it has obvious advantages: the clustering process does not have too many hypothetical requirements for data structures, while the k-means method requires data to be convex; since spectral clustering is a graph cut process, there is no case where discrete clusters are clustered together as they are for the k-means method. In addition, its computational speed for a large dataset is significantly better than other algorithms.

The core idea in spectral clustering is to set up all the data as points in space, which can be connected by edges. The edge weight of two distant points is lower, and the edge weight of the two close points is higher. The clustering process is to find a partition of the graph such that the edges between different groups have very low weights and the edges within a group have high weights. The algorithmic process of spectral clustering is given in Algorithm 1.

The spectral clustering process has two steps. The first step is to construct the data point into a graph, and the second is to extract the graph into a sub-graph, which corresponds to the clusters (Steps 1–3 in Algorithm 1). There are three constructions that transform the given data points into a similarity graph (Step 1 in Algorithm 1): the ε-neighborhood graph, the k-nearest neighborhood graph and the fully connected graph.

(1) **The ε-neighborhood graph** connects two points with a distance less than $\varepsilon ,$ and the adjacency matrix is defined as:

$$
W _ {i, j} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \text {if} s _ {i, j} > \varepsilon \\ \varepsilon , & \text {if} s _ {i, j} \leq \varepsilon \end{array} \right.\tag{1}
$$

<div class="docvortex-algorithm" style="white-space: pre-wrap; font-family:monospace;">
Algorithm 1 Spectral clustering.

Input: Dataset $D = (x_1, x_2, ..., x_n)$, number $K$ of clusters to construct, method to construct a similarity graph
Output: Cluster $C_1, C_2, ..., C_k$
Construct a similarity graph $S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ according to the method we input;
Construct the adjacency matrix $W$ and the degree matrix $D$ by $S$;
Obtain Laplacian $L$ by $L = D - W$;
Compute the first $k$ eigenvectors $u_1, u_2, ..., u_k$ of $L$.
Obtain $U = (u_1, u_2, ..., u_k), U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$;
FOR $i = 1, ..., n$, let $y_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$ be the vector corresponding to the $i$ th row of $U$;
Cluster the points $(y_i)_{i=1,...,n}$ in $\mathbb{R}^k$ with the $K$-means into clusters $C_1, C_2, ..., C_k$.
Return: Clusters $C_1, C_2, ..., C_k$
</div>

W _ {i, j} = W _ {j, i} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \text {if} x _ {i} \notin K N N \big (X _ {j} \big) \text {and} x _ {j} \notin K N N (X _ {i}) \\ \exp \left(\frac {- \left\| x _ {i} - x _ {j} \right\| ^ {2}}{2 \sigma^ {2}}\right), & \text {if} x _ {i} \in K N N \big (X _ {j} \big) \text {or} x _ {j} \in K N N (X _ {i}) \end{array} \right.\tag{2}

W _ {i, j} = W _ {j, i} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \text {if} x _ {i} \notin K N N \big (X _ {j} \big) \text {or} x _ {j} \notin K N N (X _ {i}) \\ \exp \left(\frac {- \left\| x _ {i} - x _ {j} \right\| ^ {2}}{2 \sigma^ {2}}\right), & \text {if} x _ {i} \in K N N \big (X _ {j} \big) \text {and} x _ {j} \in K N N (X _ {i}) \end{array} \right.\tag{3}
$$

(3) **The fully connected graph** connects all points with positive similarity with each other and weights all the edges by $s _ { i j } .$ The most commonly used algorithm to obtain $s _ { i j }$ is the Gaussian kernel function RBF, where the similarity matrix and the adjacency matrix are the same:

$$
W _ {i, j} = S _ {i, j} = \exp \left(\frac {- \left\| x _ {i} - x _ {j} \right\| ^ {2}}{2 \sigma^ {2}}\right)\tag{4}
$$

In Algorithm 1, Steps 4–7 are the graph cut process. There are two common methods to make a graph cut: the Ratio-cut and the N-cut. They are defined below:

$$
\text {Ratio - cut} (A _ {1}, A _ {2}, \dots A _ {K}) = \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {i} ^ {k} \frac {W \left(A _ {i} , \overline {{A}} _ {i}\right)}{\left| A _ {i} \right|}\tag{5}
$$

$$
N - c u t = (A _ {1}, A _ {2}, \dots A _ {k}) = \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {i} ^ {k} \frac {W \left(A _ {i} , \overline {{A}} _ {i}\right)}{\operatorname{vol} \left(A _ {i}\right)}\tag{6}
$$

where A is the subset of vertices after the graph cut, $W ( A _ { i } , \overline { { A } } _ { i } )$ )is the cut weight of two disjoined sets $A _ { i }$ and $\overline { { A } } _ { i } { , } | A _ { i } | \mathrm { i s }$ the number of vertices andvol $( A _ { i } )$ is the sum of the weights of all edges attached to vertices in A.

As we mentioned above, we need to find a partition to extract the graph and the best partition to minimize Ratio-cut or N-cut. Since the calculation of the minimum will lead to an NP-hard problem, the pioneers successfully convert it into a linear algebra equation. Therefore, only the first k eigenvectors of the

Laplacian matrix need to be calculated. That is, we specify the dimensionality and reduce the dimension from n to k so that the NP-hard problem can be approximately solved. Since we lose a small amount of information when using the dimension specification, we usually need to perform a traditional clustering, such as k-means, on each row after obtaining the matrix U of the $n \times k$ dimension, The specific derivation process refers to the literature (Von Luxburg, 2007), and we will not go into details here. In this paper, we use N-cut to find the minimum partition.

## 3. The proposed method

We propose a multi-class imbalanced learning algorithm in this section, which integrates the One-Versus-One (OVO) decomposition and resampling method based on spectral clustering.

3.1. One-Versus-One decomposition with spectral clustering-based sampling algorithm

As we mentioned earlier, the current method of generating new samples for imbalanced learning is simply to make an indiscriminate synthesis of the samples based on the distance between the samples. This method does not take into account the different characteristics of the data in each class. For example, in the sample of a class, a certain space may be denser, and some of the samples may be sparse. In other words, some samples may be just discrete points in a class. It is of little value to resample these unrepresentative sample points. For the imbalance problem, we focus on sampling, where denser samples occur in these spaces so that the prediction for the minority samples are more targeted. Therefore, in this paper, we use spectral clustering to classify subspaces for the minor class in the decomposed binary-class training set. For each subspace, we sample at different degrees (equal scale of each subspace) according to its density to rebalance the training set. We used the SMOTE oversampling method in this experiment.

Fig. 1 shows the workflow of the algorithm. The algorithm process can be roughly divided into three steps. First, we use the OVO decomposition method to decompose the original dataset into multiple two-class training sets. For a C-class dataset, OVO decomposes it into $C ( C \mathrm { ~ - ~ } 1 ) / 2$ binary-class subsets. Second, for each of the decomposed sub-datasets, we calculate the imbalance ratio, which is defined as the majority class divided by the minor class. According to Fernandez’s previous work on the topic (Fernández, García, del Jesus & Herrera, 2008), the training set is imbalanced if the IR has a value higher than 1.5. If the IR of the subset is less than 1.5, we handle it as a normal dataset and do not operate it; otherwise, we will perform spectral clustering on the minor class. Before the spectral clustering algorithm begins, we need to define the number of clusters cluster\_num and the number of K-neighbors k\_neigh\_sc in the construction of the similarity graph. For each cluster generated after spectral clustering, we perform oversampling at a particular ratio. This ratio is the IR of the subset obtained by OVO decomposition. It should be noted that if the quantity of minor samples is extremely small (e.g. the number of minority samples is less than 10), we directly oversample, instead of sampling after spectral clustering. Because spectral clustering is meaningless when the number of samples is extremely small. We set the threshold for this extremely small sample size to cluster\_num × k\_neigh\_sc. After the sampling is complete, we train classifiers on these balanced datasets.

Step 3: For each pair of binary class, combining the

resampled class with the original class to train a classifier

Fig. 1. Workflow of the proposed algorithm.

In the prediction phase, we feed each test sample to all trained classifiers to obtain a confidence interval for each test sample on each classifier. Since the majority-vote algorithm is the simplest and most efficient label integration method (Nicholson, Sheng & Zhang, 2016; Zhang, Sheng, Li, Wu & Wu, 2017b; 2015), we use it to combine the prediction results of each classifier to determine the final class label of the sample in the experiment. The way to generate the class label is to represent the output of each binary classifier in a code- matrix M:

$$
M (i, j) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1, & \text {if output} = i \\ 0, & \text {otherwise} \end{array} \right.\tag{7}
$$

Clearly, when M(i, j) = 1then M(i, j) = 0 and vice versa. The final class is assigned by computing the maximum vote:

$$
\text {Class} = \arg \max _ {i = 1, \dots , C} \left\{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {C} M _ {i, j} \right\}\tag{8}
$$

To clarify this procedure, the complete process is summarized in Algorithm 2.

We consider this combination because the OVO strategy is superior to OVA strategy in multi-class imbalanced learning. For resampling part, most resampling algorithms as we mentioned above do not consider the shape of the class distributions of the data so that there exist many instances lying in the intersection areas of the class boundaries. It will be more effective for model learning if the sampled the data have clear class boundaries. To explore the shape of class distributions, we perform spectral clustering that help sample the data with similar characteristics.

## 3.4. Computational complexity

The computational complexity of our proposed algorithm is mainly reflected in the sampling stage, which is based on spectral clustering. Therefore, we first consider the computational complexity of the sampling algorithm. In our algorithm, we apply spectral clustering to the minority class in each binary subset. In the spectral clustering, it takes $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ to construct the similarity matrix for all data point $X _ { n }$ in the minority class, O(n) to calculate the adjacency matrix W, the degree matrix D and the Laplacian matrix $L ,$ and O(n) to obtain the first keigenvectors $u _ { 1 } { , } u _ { 2 } { , } . . . u _ { k }$ of L. For k-means, its computational complexity is $O ( l \bullet K \bullet k \bullet n ) ,$ where k is the number of eigenvectors we defined in this study, l is the number of iterations, and K is the number of clusters. Generally, l, k and m can be considered constant. Hence, the computational complexity of the sampling method for each minority

class is

$$
O \big (n ^ {2} \big) + O (n) + O (n) + O (l \cdot K \cdot k \cdot n) = O \big (n ^ {2} \big)\tag{9}
$$

For the K clusters formed by spectral clustering, the SMOTE algorithm is performed. At this time, the computational complexity for the sampling process of each cluster is $O ( I R \bullet ( n / K ) )$ , where IR is a constant as the imbalanced ratio, so the computational complexity for the SMOTE stage is $K \bullet O ( I R \bullet ( n / K ) )$ , which can be simplified to O(n). Combined with the above analysis, the computational complexity of the whole sampling algorithm is $O ( n ^ { 2 } )   +   O ( n )$ , that is $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$

## 4. Experiments

The main objective of the experiment is to verify the effectiveness of our proposed method for solving multiclass imbalanced learning problems. In this section, we first give a brief description of the datasets, evaluation metric and competitors. Then, we present the experiment’s results and analysis.

## 4.1. Datasets

We select 11 datasets from the KEEL, UCI and OpenML dataset repository to evaluate the performance of the proposed method. Table 1 summarizes the detailed information from these datasets. Each dataset contains the number of samples (#Size), number of attributes (#Attr), number of real values (#R), number of integer values (#I), number of classes (#Cl), the imbalanced ratio (IR) and the distribution of each class. The size of the datasets ranges from 106 to 6876, while the number of attributions varies from 3 to 9, the number of classes is between 3 and 10 and the imbalanced ratio is in the interval between 1.57–109.9. In this experiment, we used a 10-fold cross-validation

## 4.2. Evaluation metrics

Accuracy is not a good metric for the imbalance problem since it often has a bias toward the majority class (Di Martino, Fernández, Iturralde & Lecumberry, 2013). Hence, we employ multiclass AUC (MAUC) (Hand & Till, 2001), the precision of minor classes $( P _ { m i n } )$ (Yang, Kuang, Zhang & Zhang, 2018) and the average precision of all classes $( P _ { a v g } )$ (Ferri, Hernández-Orallo & Modroiu, 2009; Yang et al., 2018) as metrics that can more accurately assess the performance of imbalanced learning algorithms. The MAUC is a more comprehensive metric for the multiclass imbalanced problem, which is defined as follows:

$$
\mathrm{MAUC} = \frac {2}{k (k - 1)} \sum_ {i <   j} A (i, j), \text {where} A (i, j) = (A (i | j) + A (j | i)) / 2\tag{10}
$$

Here, A(i|j) is the probability that a randomly drawn member of class j has a lower estimated probability of belonging to class i than a randomly drawn member of i-class. Note that for multiclass problems, A(i|j) and A(j|i) may not be equal.

Both $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ and $P _ { a v g }$ measure performance from a precision perspective. $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ reflects the precision of minority class with the smallest size and $P _ { a v g ^ { 1 } }$ epresents the average precision of all classes. The precision of the i th class in the experiment can be expressed as:

$$
P _ {i} = \frac {T P _ {i}}{T P _ {i} + F P _ {i}}\tag{11}
$$

where TP<sub>i</sub> (True Positive of i th class) denotes a positive sample predicted to be positive by the model in the i th class, and FP<sub>i</sub> (False Positive of i th class) denotes a negative sample predicted to be positive by the model. Correspondingly, the $P _ { a v g }$ is calculated by:

$$
P _ {a v g} = \frac {1}{c} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {c} P _ {i}\tag{12}
$$

where c is the number of class.

G-mean is the root of the product of class-wise sensitivity. This measure tries to maximize the accuracy on each of the classes while keeping these accuracies balanced. G-mean is calculated by:

$$
G - \text {mean} = \sqrt {\frac {T P}{T P + F N} + \frac {T N}{T N + F P}}\tag{13}
$$

## 4.3. The compared methods and parameter settings

In this section, we present a comparison with the competitors in the form of an experiment. To offer a good comparison with other OVO decomposition-based techniques dedicated to multiclass imbalanced learning we have selected four state-of-the-art methods: OVO strategy with SMOTE (Fernández et al., 2010), Improved All-and-One (A&O) with SMOTE (Li, Zou, Han & Xia, 2013), OVO strategy with Underbagging (Krawczyk, 2015), Multi\_IM (Ghanem, Venkatesh & West, 2010), DRCW\_ASEG (Zhang, Luo, González, García & Herrera, 2018), EasyEnsemble (Liu et al., 2009), and SMOTEBoost (Chawla et al., 2003).

• OVO-SMOTE (OSM): OVO-SMOTE is a representative technique that is a combination of a binarization technique and oversampling. This method uses SMOTE as a sampling approach after OVO decomposition.

• Improved A&O with SMOTE (IAOS): IAOS integrates the improved All-and-One (A&O) and data resample method. A&O is a combination of OVO and OVA. It first uses OVA to find two classes with the largest candidate probability. If the IR between these two classes is greater than the specified threshold, SMOTE is applied to the minority candidate. When the dataset reaches equilibrium, it will be trained to find the final winner.

• OVO-Underbagging (OUB): OVO-Underbagging combines OVO decomposition with Underbagging. UnderBagging is an ensemble algorithm that applies undersampling of the majority class conducted independently in each bag of the ensemble.

• Multi-IM: Multi-IM extends PRMs-IM to handle the multiclass classification by employing PRMs-IM in the multiclass technique A&O approach. The main idea of PRMs-IM is to extend a relational learning technique called Probability Relational Models (PRMs) to address imbalanced problems. PRMs-IM can be regarded as an ensemble of PRM models, each of which trains on a balanced subset. Each subset of data is constructed by all the samples from the minority class and an equal number of samples randomly selected from the majority class.

• DRCW\_ASEG: DRCW\_ASEG can be divided into DRCW and ASEG, where DRCW is the dynamic classifier weighting in an OVO scheme and ASEG generates synthetic examples by dynamically learning the local information from the data distribution.

• OVO-EasyEnsemble (OEE): OVO-EasyEnsemble combines OVO decomposition with EasyEnsemble. EasyEnsemble uses the ensemble learning mechanism to divide the majority class into several sub-sets for and each sub-set combines with the minority to train different learners.

• OVO-SMOTEBoost (OSB): OVO-SMOTEBoost combines OVO decomposition with SMOTEBoost. The SMOTEBoost algorithm is also an ensemble learning algorithm based on the idea of integrating SMOTE with Adaboost.M2. It introduces SMOTE at each boosting iteration.

In this experiment, the parameter settings are consistent for each dataset and each partition. The k-neigh parameter is set to 5 for any comparison method involving the SMOTE algorithm, including OVO-SMOTE, Improved A&O with SMOTE and SMOTE-Boosting. The number of base classifiers is set to 50 for any comparison method involving ensemble learning, including OVO-Underbagging, EasyEnsemble, and SMOTEBoosting. In DRCW\_ASEG, the parameter settings are: K1=5, K2=3, K3=10, and the scaling coefficient alpha is set to 0.1, where K1 is the number of nearest neighbors used to define the local region of the query example, K2 means the number of nearest neighbors in adjusting the sampling probability of the minority examples and K3 represents the number of nearest neighbors used in the dynamic weighting procedure. For all the methods in experiments, we use the CART decision tree as the base classifier, which is implemented in the famous Python machine learning library scikit-learn (version 0.19.2). We use the default parameter settings of the CART in the scikit-learn library.

## 4.4. Comparison of proposed method with other multiclass imbalanced algorithms

The results of the proposed method are presented in comparison to the OSM, IAOS, OUB, Multi-IM DRCW\_ASEG, OEE and OSB. Tables 2-5 shows the performance results of the eight approaches on 13 datasets, where the best result for each dataset is shown in bold. From the results we can see:

• For the for metrics, the OSC is the superior algorithm. The average performance of OSC obtained using the MAUC, $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } } ,$ and $P _ { a v g }$ all support this conclusion.

• The average MAUC of OSC outperforms all other methods in 8 out of 13 datasets, which verifies that OSC is significantly better than all the compared methods. In some datasets, OSC performs slightly worse than some of the other methods. For example, OSC in the New dataset is 2.24% lower than IAOS. In the Cle dataset, OSC is 0.65% lower than OEE and is 0.22% lower than OEE in the Car dataset. The gaps in these pairs of comparisons are extremely small and don’t even make a 0.1% difference. Therefore, the overall performance of the OSC is better than other competitors but the OSC may not always be optimal for resampling of some types of datasets.

• We all acknowledge that for imbalanced data, the precision of the minority classes is of great significance. More importantly, the misclassifications in the minority class cause damage to practical applications. Our proposed algorithm also shows better performance on $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } } .$ The average value of $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ exceeds the second by 5.78% and OSC shows the best performance of $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ on 9 datasets. On the Cle dataset, OSC is far ahead with a score of 16.07%, and its $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ value is even more than twice that of the second Multi\_IM. We also noticed that, although DRCW\_ASEG achieved the best performance on 3 of all datasets, second only to OSC, its average performance is inferior to OSM with only one best performance. This is due to the unstable performance of DRCW\_ASEG. For example, the performance of DRCW\_ASEG is the lowest on datasets such as Car, Cle, and Bre, even a $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ of 0 occurs on Cle.

• From $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ we can see that some datasets have a higher average precision for the minority class, while others are extremely low, and some average precisions (Cle, Win and Mar) do not exceed 20%. By analyzing the data characteristics, we discover that the low $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ value of Cle may be due to the extremely small sample of its minimum minority class, while the low performance of Win and Mar can be blamed on the large-scale sample size

and a large number of attributes. Reducing redundant featureby-feature selection may effectively improve the classification precision of imbalanced learning (Zhang, Bi & Soda, 2017a). It is worth noting that on the Hay dataset, three algorithms obtained a $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ of 100%, and the $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ values of the other algorithms are correspondingly high. It is observed that the Hay tends to be a balanced dataset with an IR of 2.09 and the number of minority class samples is relatively large; so it can also be regarded as a relatively imbalanced dataset with a more average class distribution. Therefore, we can conclude that relatively imbalanced datasets have good minority class precision and this can also be verified on the Car and UKM datasets.

• The $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ is good at identifying the minority class, while other classes may have the possibility of misclassification. However, $P _ { a v g }$ provides a comprehensive way to evaluate the precision of each class. As shown in Table 4, from the perspective of $P _ { a v g } ,$ OSC also has an absolute advantage. The OSC has eight best performances on 11 datasets, and the average is 3.5% higher than the second. It can be seen that the overall performance of the OSC is better.

• The dominant advantage of the OSC algorithm is also demonstrated by G-mean. We can clearly see that OSC wins 9 in 13 datasets. In the experiment with G-mean as the evaluation metric, the performance average of EasyEnsemble is second only to OSC, which is excellent.

• OSC outperforms on some large datasets (such as Win, Mar and Vo1), indicating that the resampling scheme proposed in this paper is suitable for processing large datasets.

• Although OSM did not get the best results on the three metrics, the average of these three metrics is second only to the method we proposed, which shows that its performance is very stable.

• The IR of datasets affects the performance of the algorithm. In general, the performance will be worse on the dataset with a larger IR. However, it also depends on the other characteristics of the dataset. Here, we take the experiment results under the $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ as an example, since $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ is an evaluation metric for the smallest minority class, and it can reflect the impact of IR on the performance of the algorithm. From the results, we can observe that on the small IR datasets such as New and Hay, all the algorithms perform well, and even five algorithms have $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ as 100%, which is in accordance with our expectations. However, for the datasets with large IR, taking Pag (IR=175.4) and Win (IR=109.9) for example, whose IRs are both 100. Performance of the algorithms on these two datasets are very different. Although the IR of Pag is greater than that of Win, the average performance of the algorithms on Pag is higher. The highest performance on Pag is 79.23%, the lowest is 27.82%, while the highest performance on Win is 17.52%, and the lowest is 0.87%. By analyzing the datasets, we found that the number of instances in the minimum class of Pag is more than that in the minimum class of Win. Therefore, the performance of large IR datasets is not necessarily poor, which also depends on the size of the sample. More instances in minor class may facilitate to train good classifiers.

## 4.5. Wilcoxon test for each pair of comparisons

To evaluate the significance of the results we obtained in Tables $2 { - } 5 ,$ we introduce a statistical test based on the non-parametric hypothesis Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare the differences among these algorithms by pairwise comparisons. The corresponding results of the Wilcoxon test are reported in Table 6. The horizontal header is the metric, the vertical header represents each group of comparison algorithms, and the values in the table are the p-values. The p-value represents the degree of difference between a pair of algorithms, allowing us to determine if they are significantly different. In this paper, we believe that the difference is significant at $p < 0 . 0 5 .$ Obviously, we can see that the p-values of 7 pairwise algorithms for MAUC and $P _ { a v g }$ are all less than 0.05, so there is a significant difference between them and the proposed algorithm OSC is obviously superior than the comparison algorithms in principle. From $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ ’s point of view, the comparison of OSC vs DRCW\_ASEG is $p { > } 0 . 0 5$ , which means that the hypothesis that there is a significant difference between these two algorithms is rejected.

## 4.6. Comparison by 10-Ford stratified cross-validation

We use stratified cross-validation as the dataset partitioning strategy. It ensures that the proportions of the samples in the training set and test set are the same as those in the original dataset. It is particularly effective in imbalanced learning since it ensures that minority samples can be distributed in both the training set and the test set. In this experiment, we run 10 times stratified 10-fold CV, whose results are shown in Tables 7–10.

Although these experimental results are not statistically identical to the k-fold cross-validation, they are inherently consistent. The OSC algorithm still has tremendous advantages in these datasets. As for the MAUC metric, OSC wins on the Hay dataset but loses 1.84% on Pag dataset comparing with OUB. Overall, its average performance is still ranked first. From the perspective of $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } } ,$ our OSC method also wins on ten datasets, even obtaining 100% of $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ on Vo1. We also have consistent observations in $P _ { a v g }$ and G-Mean. Therefore, under both data partitioning strategies, the performance of OSC is superior to others.

## 4.7. Comparison using different clustering methods

To verify the impact of different clustering methods on the learning performance, we replaced the spectral clustering in our proposed algorithm with K-means. The parameter settings are consistent with our proposed algorithm. We performed our experiments on the 13 datasets with four evaluation metrics.

The experimental results in Table 11 show that the sampling algorithm with spectral clustering has an overwhelming advantage over the sampling algorithm with k-means. The spectral clusteringbased algorithm performed better than k-means-based algorithm on each of the evaluation metrics for each dataset, except that on Hay, they all achieved 100% of $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } } .$ The average performance of the sampling algorithm with spectral clustering is higher than kmeans by at least 4%−6% on four evaluation metrics. This experiment demonstrates the importance of spectral clustering in our algorithms.

## 4.9. Comparison of with OVO-without-resampling method

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

In this subsection, we compare our algorithm with the OVO-without-resampling algorithm. The OVO-without-resampling algorithm trains (OVO–NS) each subset directly after the OVO decomposition. The basic classifier used here is the same as the classifier used in all the experiments above (i.e., the CART decision tree). From the experimental results (shown Table 13), we find that our algorithm is greatly improved compared with the non-sampling algorithm, which wins on all datasets in four evaluation metrics.

## 4.11. Analysis of OSC behavior according to the degree of IR threshold

For the OSC algorithm, we modify the IR threshold to verify the stability of the algorithm, where IR increases from 1.2 to 2.7 in steps of 0.3. Since we already have four datasets whose IR value is less than 2.7, the threshold of IR does not need to be increased any more. In Figs. 5–7, we use a box plot to visually show the values of MAUC, $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } } ,$ and $P _ { a v g }$ at different IR thresholds. In the figure, the solid red line indicates the median of each metric, while the green dotted line indicates the means. The specific values can be found in Tables 6–8. From Figs. 5–7, we can clearly see that with the change of IR, the three metrics have a slight advantage when the IR value is 1.5. We simply sort the mean performance of each metric on a different IR degree. It can be seen that the lowest mean performance among the three metrics is at the IR degree of 2.4, 2.1 and 2.7, respectively. That is, the larger the IR threshold is set, the slightly lower the performance of the algorithm. Since our algorithm only addresses the dataset when its imbalanced ratio reaches the IR threshold we set, it can reflect that it is a reasonable choice to define a dataset with an imbalance ratio greater than 1.5 as an imbalanced dataset.

On the other hand, with the increase of IR, the change in MAUC, whose means and medians are basically kept at a uniform level, is not obvious. The difference of 1.22% from the largest and smallest MAUC can confirm our conclusion. Furthermore, $P _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ only slightly floats higher as well, and the situation is roughly the same as $P _ { a v g } ,$ In summary, the algorithm has superior stability with varied IR degrees.

## 5. Conclusion

This paper presented a new method for the classification of multiclass imbalanced data. The proposed method combines an OVO decomposition strategy with a spectral clustering-based resampling technique. We evaluated the performance of the proposed method by the comparisons with seven state-of-the-art algorithms on 13 multiclass imbalanced datasets. The experimental results confirm the superiority of our method in solving the multiclass imbalanced problems.
